title: A bounded pool with named threads

blocks.text: The page warns that `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` queues without limit, and recommends building a `ThreadPoolExecutor` yourself: a **bounded** queue, a rejection policy, and a `ThreadFactory` that gives the threads useful names. Its interview answer walks a pool of core 2, maximum 4 and a queue of 2 through seven tasks.
Write `BoundedPool.create(core, max, queueCapacity, name)`, returning a `ThreadPoolExecutor` that:

items: keeps `core` threads (idle core threads do not time out) and grows to at most `max` threads;
refuses a task it cannot take by throwing `RejectedExecutionException`;

names its threads `name-1`, `name-2`, ... in the order it creates them, as daemon threads. (Threads may be created from several submitting threads at once, so count them thread-safely; the tests submit from one thread, so they cannot catch a racy count.)

rows: names of the threads running the first 6 tasks

cases.says: The first tasks start core threads, and the next ones wait in the queue.
Threads beyond the core size start only once the bounded queue is full.
A task that finds the pool at its maximum and the queue full is refused with RejectedExecutionException.
Each pool's threads are daemons named after the pool, numbered from 1 in every new pool.
The pool keeps its core threads when idle: core 2 and maximum 4 as asked, and core threads never time out.

concepts: With the default AbortPolicy, a task that finds the pool and the queue full is refused with RejectedExecutionException.
A production pool is built directly with a bounded queue and a rejection policy, instead of the unbounded queue of newFixedThreadPool.
A ThreadPoolExecutor starts core threads first, then queues, and starts threads beyond the core size only once the queue is full.
A custom ThreadFactory names the pool's threads and can make them daemons, so thread dumps are readable.
